transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-18
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Leah Ortiz (CSM); Priya Patel (Nimbus PM), Samir Kapoor (Nimbus Lead Eng), Joan Lee (Nimbus SRE), Ethan Morris (Nimbus Data Eng)

Summary (auto): quick POC sync to review weekend run, discuss serialization failures in function-calling, tune SDK invocation patterns, decide next steps for a short latency lab.

[00:00] Avery Chen: okay everyone thanks for joining, last week we kicked off the small pilot, wanted to go over the results, a few failure modes Samir raised and then talk about tuning the SDK usage for more stable structured output.
[00:18] Priya Patel: yes thanks Avery, quick context — our core use-case is triage of inbound patient messages, so we need deterministic JSON output for downstream systems, also tight latency (sub 700ms token to first byte ideally) but we can trade a bit of cost if reliability improves.
[00:34] Marco Ruiz: perfect, that matches what we saw in the results — overall throughput is fine, token cost is in-line, but we saw a bunch of serialization mismatches when function-calling was used in the same prompt as freeform text.
[00:50] Samir Kapoor: right — about 14% of completions returned malformed JSON, or extra commentary outside the JSON block. In our logs it looks like the model occasionally appended clarifying text after the final brace. It's intermittent.
[01:12] Marco Ruiz: yeah, that's the classic stray text problem. Two levers we recommend: 1) enforce stricter structured-output via the SDK's schema enforcement wrapper, and 2) if you can, use function-calling-only flows for critical paths — that reduces hallucinated prose.
[01:31] Joan Lee: quick question — when you say "SDK schema enforcement" is that a runtime validator or do you do retry/patching inside the request? We're worried about extra latency if you add validation.
[01:45] Marco Ruiz: it's a lightweight validator on the client. Pattern is: Redwood returns a candidate; SDK attempts to parse/validate; if parsing fails, SDK will optionally call the model again with a brief prompt to fix the JSON (auto-repair) or return an explicit parse error to the app. The auto-repair is configurable — for production-critical flows we recommend the explicit error + fallback to a simpler model variant for quick recovery.
[02:11] Ethan Morris: can we see a code snippet? our pipelines are Python heavy.
[02:15] Marco Ruiz: yes I'll share 2 snippets — one using the function-calling API with a strict JSON schema, and one showing the parse/repair loop. For example, in Python you'd do: client.invoke(functions=[...], schema=expected_schema, repariter=null) — sorry the exact param names will be in the snippet I share, this is verbal.
[02:38] Priya Patel: cool. Also Samir pinged that sometimes the KV cache is leaking across user sessions in the sandbox — is that a Redwood thing or our integration bug?
[02:51] Samir Kapoor: it looked like contexts from previous conversations influenced later completion choices, causing wrong triage categories. We can't have cross-user state.
[03:03] Marco Ruiz: KV cache should be per-session by default unless you explicitly enable cross-session prefix caching. The sandbox team likely enabled a shared prefix during the weekend run to speed up cold starts. I'll check the pilot config and flag it. If it's enabled, that would explain the leakage.
[03:18] Joan Lee: that would make sense. Please confirm since our compliance team will flag any cross-user mixing.
[03:24] Marco Ruiz: absolutely — I'll confirm and paste the exact config.
[03:29] Leah Ortiz: quick note — we also observed a small latency bump when you pass large user profile blobs in the prompt. Consider using reference keys + the Redwood cache to store large textual context instead of inlining.
[03:44] Samir Kapoor: noted. On the serialization failures: sometimes the model returns single quotes instead of double quotes, or trailing commas — parser is strict so it fails. Any heuristics to avoid that?
[03:57] Marco Ruiz: common ones: 1) provide explicit examples in the system prompt (few-shot with valid JSON), 2) use the JSON schema enforcement flag in the SDK we mentioned, 3) for sensitive flows use the model variant with higher decoding constraints — the one we ran weekend has a tunable "json_mode" that reduces allowed non-JSON tokens. That variant increases token use slightly but reduces malformed output.
[04:26] Priya Patel: is that the quantized variant you referenced? we saw a cost delta in the CSV Avery sent.
[04:32] Avery Chen: yes — the quantized v2 reduces GPU footprint by about 30% and cost per token fell, but it increases sampling quirks in some cases; we used a mild quantization profile. For structured output we recommend the non-quantized or a quant-profile with stricter sampling constraints. We'll show the numbers.
[04:51] Ethan Morris: can we get a table — latency, cost, malformed-% for each variant? the attachment in the pilot-run-results.csv had the raw rows but we want an aggregate.
[04:59] Avery Chen: yes I'll upload an aggregated sheet.
[05:05] Marco Ruiz: on SDK usage patterns — two flavors customers commonly use: 1) direct generate with post-parse validation, 2) function-calling where the model returns a function call object that maps to a strongly typed schema. For your critical triage path we think function-calling + server-side validation is best.
[05:23] Samir Kapoor: how do retries interact with idempotency? if the SDK auto-repairs and calls again, we'd rather not have duplicate downstream effects (e.g., duplicate tickets).
[05:33] Marco Ruiz: good point. The SDK attaches a client-provided idempotency key per request and failed parse responses set a retry flag. We recommend the app generate an idempotency token and if the SDK does an auto-repair it will not trigger downstream side-effects until the app explicitly commits the resulting JSON. So app pattern: call -> validate -> present to app -> app commits. That avoids duplicates.
[06:02] Priya Patel: sounds good. Next, we ran a quick stress bench — at medium concurrency (20 concurrent users) we see occasional 5xxs. Is that capacity or SDK timeout?
[06:14] Marco Ruiz: likely a combination. Redwood Dedicated gives predictable throughput; hosted can burst but you might hit soft limits. The errors in the logs — are they 502 gateway or 429 rate-limit?
[06:24] Ethan Morris: mostly 502s with a small amount of 503. The timestamps align with some big batch jobs we ran in the same region.
[06:33] Marco Ruiz: that suggests transient region overload. Two mitigations: 1) configure automatic fallback to a lower-cost variant in a different region, or 2) use the SDK retry policy with exponential backoff and a jitter. For low-latency critical paths, we recommend Dedicated or reserved capacity.
[06:51] Priya Patel: procurement is sensitive to monthly committed spend but we can negotiate a small Reserved for the pilot if it guarantees latency.
[07:00] Avery Chen: we can propose a short-term Dedicated burst plan for your pilot week. I'll include costs in the pricing note.
[07:07] Samir Kapoor: back to serialization — can Redwood's runtime enforce closing braces or sanitized JSON? I've seen post-processing tools that strip stray text.
[07:17] Marco Ruiz: we can enable a server-side sanitization hook that strips text outside the first top-level JSON block and attempts a minimal repair. It's offered as an option but with a caveat — it masks model failure modes. For compliance you might prefer failing loudly so you can track regressions.
[07:34] Joan Lee: agreed — we'd prefer failures so we can capture them in Sentry and review.
[07:40] Leah Ortiz: on a related note: set up alerting on malformed-% spikes, we'll send a default rule.
[07:46] Marco Ruiz: noted. We'll also attach per-route per-model metrics for malformed responses.
[07:52] Priya Patel: how about function-calling schema evolution? our triage schema may change as we add fields. How do we manage rollouts without breaking clients?
[08:02] Marco Ruiz: Redwood supports versioned schemas; you can pin a model+schema pair per route and do canary rollouts. The console lets you route x% of traffic to new schema and keep the rest on the previous version. If a schema mismatch occurs we can auto-fallback.
[08:17] Samir Kapoor: good. We'll want an A/B with 5% new schema for a week.
[08:22] Avery Chen: noted.
[08:25] Ethan Morris: quick curiosity, competitors — we benchmarked a small flow against OpenAI and Anthropic, results were similar but Redwood's SDK tooling made retries and schema checks simpler.
[08:36] Marco Ruiz: happy to help with a side-by-side reproducible benchmark if you want to share the harness.
[08:42] Priya Patel: yes we'll share the harness.
[08:45] Marco Ruiz: final technical note — when you're using function-calling and large context, tune batch size and the KV cache TTL. For triage, short TTLs (5-10m) avoid stale context; for persistent user sessions you can store reference keys server-side.
[08:59] Priya Patel: what about cost/levers? if we tighten decoding constraints and disable mild quantization, what's the expected cost bump?
[09:07] Avery Chen: our weekend run: non-quantized with strict json_mode raised per-token cost by about 18% but malformed rates dropped from 14% to under 1%. Quantized strict profile had ~8% cost increase but still some tail issues. We'll share the exact rows.
[09:22] Samir Kapoor: acceptable trade if we can keep latency under 700ms P50.
[09:27] Marco Ruiz: to hit that latency, we can recommend two things: 1) pin the route to the lower-latency model family, 2) use per-request early-stopping and streaming-first-byte heuristics so you get TTFB faster.
[09:41] Joan Lee: streaming is important for UX, will streaming interact with function-calling?
[09:47] Marco Ruiz: streaming will stream the function-call tokens until the model emits the end-of-call token; parse/validate still applies. You might see partial tokens but the SDK buffers until it can parse. It's supported.
[09:59] Priya Patel: okay what's the plan for the week?
[10:02] Avery Chen: plan we agreed: Redwood will run a 24h targeted pilot with non-quantized strict json_mode on a subset of flows; Marco will deliver SDK snippets and the parse/repair options; Nimbus will share failing examples and the benchmark harness. We'll schedule a 30-45m lab next week focused on latency with Joan and Samir.
[10:20] Priya Patel: sounds good. Also please include any compliance docs (SOC2 scope) since our legal asked.
[10:27] Avery Chen: will attach the security pack.
[10:30] Leah Ortiz: one last note — I'll add a follow-up where Redwood posts the perf-deck and a short how-to for onboarding the SDK to your repo.
[10:38] Samir Kapoor: thanks — sorry one more technical oddity: some responses included language like "I can't do that" before the JSON. Could that be system prompt interference?
[10:48] Marco Ruiz: yes, that's usually the safety or system instruction kicking in; for private triage flows, we can tune the system prompt and safety policy or use a model variant with tighter system allowances for enterprise customers. We'll document the tradeoffs.
[11:03] Priya Patel: ok thanks team.
[11:06] Avery Chen: recap: Marco shares SDK snippets and server-side sanitization options; Avery uploads aggregated CSV + perf-deck; Samir shares failing examples + firewall details from Joan; schedule latency lab for next week.
[11:22] Priya Patel: thanks all, talk soon.

End of transcript.
